abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: Low equivalent series resistance (ESR) is critical for high-rate energy storage devices (e.g., supercapacitors), and graphene is a promising additive for reducing ESR in carbon-based supercapacitor electrodes. However, graphene can be costly and difficult to produce at scale. This study investigates the addition of graphene, produced through electrochemical exfoliation of domestic coal-derived graphite, in activated carbon-based supercapacitors. The coal-derived graphene was incorporated at varying weight loadings and tested in symmetric supercapacitors with aqueous electrolytes. ESR was evaluated using both direct current internal resistance (DCIR) and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) measurements. DCIR measurements revealed ESR reductions of ∼34%, ∼18%, and ∼21% at 3, 5, and 10 wt % loadings, respectively, compared to the baseline (0 wt %) of ∼0.54 Ω. These results were further confirmed by EIS measurements. Correspondingly, power density increased by ∼52%, ∼27%, and ∼35% at 3, 5, and 10 wt % loadings relative to the baseline (∼29 kW/kg). Additionally, the electrodes exhibited moderate increases in specific capacitance and energy density, along with stable cycling performance (capacitance retention above 85% after 100,000 cycles) and capacitive behavior (α = 0.95–0.97), suggesting favorable charge transfer kinetics. These findings highlight the potential of exfoliated coal-derived graphene as an effective additive for supercapacitor electrodes.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p:
Energy storage is becoming more critical as large-scale renewable energy projects come online. Electrochemical energy storage (EES) systems, particularly supercapacitors, are widely studied due to their efficiency, reliability, and environmental benefits. Supercapacitors are especially attractive for their high power density, fast charge–discharge rates, and long cycle life. −
Supercapacitors can operate on two distinct mechanisms, or a combination of the two: (a) electric double-layer capacitance (EDLC), based on electrostatic charge accumulation at the electrode–electrolyte interface, (b) pseudocapacitance from Faradaic redox reactions. ,

The internal resistance of an electrochemical device is an important factor that directly affects its performance. In supercapacitors, this internal resistance is often referred to as the equivalent series resistance (ESR). The key factors that contribute to ESR are the interfacial resistance between neighboring parts of the device, including the electrode–current collector interface, electrode–electrolyte interface, and connections among active and inactive materials. The resistance is also associated with ion transport in the electrodes and electrolyte, and the resistance encountered by ions as they pass through the separator.

Engineering the electrode to possess certain properties could reduce the internal resistance. High electrical conductivity supports efficient charge transfer, and a well-developed porous structure facilitates shorter ion diffusion paths, reducing ion transport resistance. −
Various porous carbon structures utilizing graphene, carbon nanotubes, carbon nanofibers, and variations of activated carbon (AC) have been studied for their potential as EDLC electrode materials. −
ACs have long been the preferred materials for fabricating supercapacitor electrodes due to their affordability, large specific surface area, and excellent long-term stability. , However, their electrochemical performance is highly dependent on their pore structure, and, due to their defective and disordered structure, the conductivity of ACs is lower than that of highly ordered, graphitic carbon materials. ,

Graphene, by contrast, composed entirely of sp2-hybridized carbon atoms arranged in a two-dimensional structure, has garnered significant research interest owing to its high electrical and thermal conductivity, mechanical strength, large theoretical specific surface area, and strong chemical stability. ,,−
However, several challenges still need to be addressed. Graphene sheets are prone to agglomeration and restacking due to strong van der Waals forces and π–π interactions, which significantly reduce their accessible surface area, effective specific capacitance, and electrical conductivity. Additionally, the synthesis processes for graphene are often complex and expensive, which restricts its potential for large-scale applications. To address these limitations, the integration of graphene into AC-based electrodes has been proposed as a viable approach to enhance their electrochemical performance. The combination leverages the high conductivity of graphene to compensate for the poor conductivity of ACs, while also preserving a favorable porous structure for ion transport.

Graphene can be synthesized through a variety of methods. One promising top-down approach is the electrochemical exfoliation of graphite, in which ions are intercalated between the individual sheets, causing expansion of interlayer spacing and eventually exfoliation to graphene. However, the production of graphene from this method faces challenges, particularly the availability of graphite as the feedstock. Graphite is in high demand, particularly as a key component in lithium-ion batteries. For example, the United States relies almost entirely on trade for its graphite supply. As a promising domestic alternative, coal-derived graphite exhibits favorable graphitization and electrical conductivity, making it suitable for electrochemical exfoliation. Despite its potential, limited studies have explored coal-derived graphite for graphene production, and even fewer have evaluated its performance in practical device applications.

Previous studies have reported incorporating graphene into carbon-based supercapacitor electrodes; however, most systems rely on graphene oxide (GO) or GO-derived materials obtained through chemical reduction, hydrothermal treatment, doping, or other modification strategies ,,−
for coin-cell supercapacitors and −
for two-electrode supercapacitors. The synthesis route influences defect density, conductivity, surface functionality, and interlayer structure, which directly affect electrochemical performance. In this work, graphene produced by electrochemical exfoliation of coal-derived graphite without further modification is evaluated as an additive in activated carbon electrodes, and the resulting performance improvement is quantified through direct comparison with a baseline electrode fabricated and tested under identical conditions. While graphene-based supercapacitors are promising, an optimum graphene–AC ratio is required, as excessive graphene loading can reduce devices’ performance, as shown in recent works. ,,,

Therefore, exfoliated coal-derived graphene is incorporated into activated carbon electrodes at 0, 3, 5, and 10 wt % to determine the graphene content that maximizes supercapacitor performance. The electrochemical behavior is evaluated in symmetric coin cells with KOH electrolyte using cyclic voltammetry (CV), galvanostatic charge–discharge (GCD), and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS). ESR is determined using both electrochemical impedance spectroscopy and direct current internal resistance (DCIR) measurements. Long-term cycling stability is also assessed over 100,000 charge–discharge cycles, which exceeds the cycle numbers commonly reported in graphene additive studies (typically 5,000–10,000 cycles ,,−
).

sec.title: Chemical and Materials
sec.p: Activated carbon and polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) were purchased from MSE Supplies (Tucson, AZ), and MTI Corporation (Richmond, CA), respectively. N-methyl-2-pyrrolidone (NMP, biotech grade, ≥ 99.00%) was purchased from Sigma–Aldrich. All materials were used as received without further purification. The graphene used in this study was electrochemically exfoliated coal-derived graphene produced in our laboratory. For the exfoliation process, graphitized foamed coal supplied by CONSOL Innovations were used as the working electrode, while a platinum mesh served as both the counter and reference electrode. More details about the electrochemical exfoliation procedure and characterization of coal-derived graphene can be found in this group’s previous work. In the present study, nitrogen adsorption–desorption analysis was performed to evaluate the pore characteristics. The coal-derived graphene exhibited average pore diameters in the range of 15.45–25.29 nm based on the (Brunauere-Emmette-Teller) BET method and 26.55–35.95 nm based on the (Barrett–Joyner–Halenda) BJH method, indicating a predominantly mesoporous structure.

sec.title: Electrode Preparation and Cell Assembly
sec.p: An electrode slurry was prepared by mixing 94 wt % active material with 6 wt % PVDF binder dissolved in NMP. The active material was formulated in four different compositions as listed in Table S1, incorporating varying amounts of graphene (0, 3, 5, and 10 wt %) with AC. The mixture was homogenized using a FlackTek 330–100 PRO mechanical stirrer at 3000 rpm for 2 min to ensure uniform dispersion of components. The resulting slurry was coated onto nickel foil using the doctor blade method, targeting a wet film thickness of approximately 25 μm. The electrodes were dried at 80 °C for 24 h to remove residual solvent. After drying, the electrodes were compressed using a roller press to ensure uniform thickness and then punched into discs. These discs were used to assemble CR2032 coin cells in a symmetric two-electrode configuration. A borosilicate glass microfiber membrane with a 0.6 μm pore size was employed as the separator, and 6 M KOH was used as the electrolyte. The cells were sealed using an MSK-110 hydraulic crimping machine. Following assembly, the cells were allowed to rest overnight to ensure electrolyte wetting.

sec.title: Electrochemical Measurement
sec.p: Cyclic voltammetry (CV) measurements were conducted at scan rates ranging from 5 to 100 mV/s, with a voltage window of 0–1 V. Galvanostatic charge–discharge (GCD) tests were subsequently performed at currents from 5 to 100 mA, corresponding to ∼0.3–7 A/g for our electrodes. Direct current internal resistance (DCIR) testing was also conducted between GCD cycles, applying current steps from 5 to 100 mA (0.3–7 A/g) with a pulse duration of 1 ms to evaluate dynamic resistance under transient load conditions. Cycling stability was also assessed over 100,000 GCD cycles at 50 mA. CV, GCD, and DCIR were conducted using an Arbin LBT21084 battery tester. Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) was performed separately using a Gamry Interface 5000E instrument across a frequency range of 100 kHz to 1 Hz, with an AC current amplitude of 0.01 A (rms).

Among the commonly used techniques for electrochemical characterizationCV, GCD, and EISeach offers unique advantages for resistance analysis. In this study, both DCIR and EIS were performed to determine ESR. EIS is particularly effective for deconvoluting resistance contributions from the electrode, electrolyte, and interface through Nyquist plots, while DCIR provides a practical measurement based on current pulse. Resistance values from EIS are typically lower than those from current interruption or charge/discharge methods. Detailed studies show EIS-based power estimates can be up to ten times higher than those measured at 95% energy efficiency by USABC and IEC standards. , This discrepancy is often overlooked when translating lab data to real-world use. sec.title: Results and Discussion
sec.p: To evaluate the impact of incorporating exfoliated coal-derived graphene into activated carbon (AC)-based electrodes, symmetric supercapacitor coin cells (CR2032 type) were assembled using 6 M KOH electrolyte. The electrochemical performance of these devices was assessed through CV, GCD, DCIR, ESR, and cycling stability analyses. Finally, the performance of the coal-derived graphene-based electrodes was compared with previously reported literature.

sec.title: CV Analysis
sec.p: The CV profiles of both the baseline and graphene-based electrodes (Figures S1 and 1a) display a rectangular shape, which is indicative of typical EDLC behavior and the absence of pseudocapacitance. This ideal capacitive behavior is further supported by EIS results, where the constant phase element (CPE) exponent α values are high across all samples; ranging from 0.95 to 0.97 for exfoliated coal-derived graphene, indicating a nearly ideal capacitive response and minimal deviation from ideal double-layer behavior. Complementing this, Figure b shows the current response at a fixed voltage (∼0.50 V) as a function of scan rate. The linear increase of current with scan rate in both figures confirms the ideal capacitive characteristic, demonstrating that charging current scales directly with scan rate. As shown in Figure S1, the CVs retain their rectangular shape with increasing scan rates, indicating good rate capability of the electrode material.

caption.p: (a) CV curves at a scan rate of 50 mV/s, (b) current versus scan rate for coin cell supercapacitors with electrodes containing varying percentages of exfoliated coal-derived graphene.

sec.title: GCD Analysis
sec.p: Specific capacitance and energy density values for electrodes with 0, 3, 5, and 10 wt % exfoliated coal-derived graphene loadings across various current levels are reported in Tables S2 and S3. To emphasize the relative improvements, Table summarizes the percentage changes in these values at 50 mA compared to the baseline electrode (0 wt % graphene). In addition, a representative symmetric coin cell was used for GCD analysis. Figure S1 shows GCD curves for all graphene loadings. For direct comparison at 50 mA, GCD curves for all electrodes are shown in Figure .

caption.title: Effect of Exfoliated Coal-Derived Graphene Loading on Electrochemical Properties at 50 mA (3 A/g): Average % Change from 6 Coin Cells

caption.p: GCD curves at 50 mA for coin cell supercapacitors with electrodes containing varying percentages of exfoliated coal-derived graphene.

sec.p: Regarding specific capacitance, a key indicator of energy storage capability, all electrodes demonstrated moderate values between ∼13 and 17 F/g across the tested currents. As shown in Table (at 50 mA), 3 wt % exfoliated coal-derived graphene showed a ∼5% improvement, indicating overall positive impacts from graphene inclusion. This may be due to the greater porosity and conjugation structure of graphene, which improves fast ion movements during the charge–discharge process. In contrast, electrodes with higher graphene loadings exhibited slightly lower capacitance values, showing a similar trend to the findings of Redondo et al.

A similar trend was observed for energy density, which was highest at lower currents and decreased at higher currents. At a low current of 5 mA, all electrode compositions exhibited relatively similar energy densities, ranging from 2.31 to 2.39 Wh/kg, with the highest values observed for electrodes containing 3 and 5 wt % exfoliated coal-derived graphene. As summarized in Table , at a constant current of 50 mA, the inclusion of graphene generally enhanced energy storage capabilities.

The GCD profiles of both the baseline and electrodes with some graphene content (Figures S1 and 2c) display nearly ideal triangular shapes, consistent with electrostatic charge storage typical of EDLCs. Additionally, the similarity in charging and discharging durations points to high Coulombic efficiency.

sec.title: DCIR Analysis
sec.p: Tables S2 and S3 present the ESR and power density results for electrodes containing 0, 3, 5, and 10 wt % of exfoliated coal-derived graphene. These tables provide the measured values under various current conditions for each composition, and each data point represents the average from at least five independent cells. For a clearer comparison of the effect of graphene incorporation, Table summarizes the percentage changes in ESR and power density at 50 mA, relative to the baseline electrode (0 wt % graphene).

As shown in Tables S2 and S3, ESR values remained stable across different current levels. The baseline electrode exhibited the highest resistance (∼0.54 Ω). The addition of graphene reduced ESR in all samples, with values ranging from 0.36 Ω to 0.43 Ω. Table shows that electrodes with 3 wt % graphene showed the greatest reduction in internal resistance (∼34%). The 5 wt % samples showed a slight increase in ESR compared to 3 wt % but still lower than 0 wt % baseline samples. This is further confirmed by EIS analysis, which showed that graphene-loaded electrodes (particularly at 3 wt %) exhibited reduced ESR.

The baseline electrode without graphene showed the lowest values (∼28.68–29.07 kW/kg, Table S2). The incorporation of exfoliated coal-derived graphene enhanced power density relative to the baseline. At 50 mA, 3 wt % exfoliated coal-derived graphene provided a ∼ 51.8% boost (Table ). The highest absolute values were recorded for 3 wt % exfoliated coal-derived graphene (42.09–42.74 kW/kg, Table S3). The higher power density observed with graphene incorporation can be attributed to reductions in ESR.

sec.title: EIS Analysis
sec.p: Nyquist plots for electrodes containing exfoliated coal-derived graphene are presented in Figure . The ESR, estimated from the high-frequency x-intercept of the Nyquist plot, was influenced by the incorporation of graphene. The baseline electrode (0 wt %) exhibited an ESR of approximately 0.48 Ω. Adding the exfoliated coal-derived graphene (Figure ) reduced the ESR from ∼0.48 Ω (baseline) to ∼0.23 Ω, 0.28 Ω, and 0.27 Ω for 3, 5, and 10 wt % loadings, respectively. This reduction in ESR observed via EIS measurements aligns well with the ESR values determined from DCIR analysis (Tables S2, S3 and), confirming the consistency between the two methods.

caption.p: Nyquist plot from EIS measurement for coin-cell supercapacitors with electrodes containing varying percentages of exfoliated coal-derived graphene.

sec.p: To validate the findings, EIS data for the coin cell supercapacitors were analyzed using an equivalent circuit model, R S–(CPE1 || R ct–Wo1), where R S is ESR, CPE1 is a constant phase element representing the double-layer capacitance and surface heterogeneities, R ct is the charge transfer resistance, and Wo1 accounts for ion diffusion through the porous electrode. Fitting was performed using Python’s impedance.py library (Figure S2). In the Nyquist plot, the high-to-mid frequency semicircle corresponds to R ct and CPE1. Due to deviations from ideality, CPE is used instead of a pure capacitor to account for factors like electrode roughness and pore distribution. The CPE has two parameters: α (ideal behavior) and C (capacitance). A value of α = 1 indicates ideal capacitive behavior, while α = 0.9–1 is typical for EDLCs with porous surfaces. At lower frequencies, the slope of the inclined line represents the Warburg impedance. A steeper slope indicates efficient electric double-layer formation, whereas a smaller slope suggests ion diffusion limitations. Warburg elements yield two parameters: W-R (diffusion resistance) and W-T (diffusion time constant). For finite-length diffusion, the W-T parameter is defined as W−T=L2D , where L is the diffusion length of cations within the electrode and D is their chemical diffusivity.

The fitted parameters for all samples are summarized in Table . The CPE1-derived α values increased with graphene addition. The baseline electrode exhibited an α of 0.91. Exfoliated coal-derived graphene showed higher α values at all loadings: 0.97 at 3 wt %, 0.95 at 5 wt %, and 0.97 at 10 wt %, indicating nearly ideal capacitive behavior.

caption.title: Fitted EIS Parameters for Different Coin Cell Supercapacitor Samples

sec.p: Charge transfer resistance (R ct) also varied depending on the loading of graphene. The baseline electrode showed the R ct value of 0.16 Ω. The 3 wt % exfoliated coal-derived graphene electrode exhibited a higher R ct of 0.20 Ω. However, R ct decreased with increasing exfoliated coal-derived graphene content, reaching 0.17 Ω at 5 wt % and further down to 0.13 Ω at 10 wt %, the lowest among all samples. Despite having a higher R ct at 3 wt %, exfoliated coal-derived graphene consistently exhibited lower ESR and higher α values across all concentrations.

Diffusion resistance (Wo1 R) and time constant (Wo1 T) also varied. The baseline electrode had a diffusion resistance of 0.21 Ω and a time constant of 0.05 s. At 3 wt %, exfoliated coal-derived graphene showed higher diffusion resistance (0.28 Ω) but the same time constant (0.05 s). At 5 wt %, exfoliated coal-derived graphene demonstrated improved diffusion: 0.16 Ω and 0.04 s. At 10 wt %, exfoliated coal-derived graphene maintained slightly higher resistance (0.17 Ω) but a similarly low time constant (0.04 s).

sec.title: Stability Analysis
sec.p: Long-term stability tests were performed on the electrodes containing different loadings (3, 5, and 10 wt %) of exfoliated coal-derived graphene over 100,000 charge–discharge cycles using the GCD method at a constant current of 50 mA, as shown in Figure .

caption.p: (a) ESR and (b) specific capacitance as a function of cycle number for coin cell supercapacitors with electrodes containing varying percentages of exfoliated coal-derived graphene.

sec.p: Figure a shows the ESR as a function of cycle number. After 1,00,000 cycles, the ESR increased only slightly from 0.24 to 0.25 Ω for the 3 wt % electrode, from 0.27 to 0.39 Ω for the 5 wt % electrode, and from 0.28 to 0.36 Ω for the 10 wt % electrode. The loss of behavior (LOB), typically defined as the point at which ESR doubles from its initial value, was not reached for any electrode.

Capacitance retention data are shown in Figure b. Capacitance retention further confirms the long-term stability of all electrodes, as the LOB refers to the point at which the capacitance retention drops to 80%. Electrodes with 3, 5, and 10 wt % graphene exhibited stable cycling, retaining 97.80%, 85.39%, and 89.54% of their initial capacitance, respectively, after 100,000 cycles. However, the results indicate that increasing graphene content beyond the optimal level does not necessarily enhance cycling stability.

sec.title: Performance Comparison
sec.p: To benchmark the electrodes containing some coal-derived graphene, performance was compared to previously reported graphene-based coin cell devices, as summarized in Table . Capacitors fabricated using 3 wt % electrochemically exfoliated coal-derived graphene showed lower specific capacitance than rGO-based systems reported in the literature. However, they exhibited lower ESR, which contributed to higher power output and faster charge–discharge behavior. The devices also maintained stable performance over 100,000 cycles, indicating potentially better long-term durability compared to earlier studies. These results suggest that coal-derived graphene, while having lower capacitance, can still provide practical advantages in terms of rate capability and power delivery in aqueous electrolyte systems.

caption.title: Comparison of the Devices in this Work with Reported Graphene-Based Coin Cell Supercapacitors Based on Electrode Mass

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: This study investigates the electrochemical performance of supercapacitor electrodes incorporating different loadings of exfoliated coal-derived graphene, produced from domestic coal-derived graphite foam via a simple anodic exfoliation technique using an aqueous electrolyte. The results show that graphene enhances the performance of activated carbon-based electrodes. At 3 wt %, electrodes demonstrated the lowest ESR.

DCIR results show that electrodes with 3, 5, and 10 wt % exfoliated coal-derived graphene reduced ESR by 18–34% compared to the baseline. Power density increased, with 3, 5, and 10 wt % samples reaching improvements of about ∼52%, ∼27%, and ∼35%, respectively. Specific capacitance and energy density also increased, with 3 and 5 wt % loadings increasing by approximately 3.3–5%, while 10 wt % showed a slightly lower gain (∼2.3%). EIS analysis confirmed reduced ESR, with the lowest ESR (0.23 Ω) at 3 wt % loading. Furthermore, exfoliated coal-derived graphene electrodes demonstrated excellent cycling stability, retaining over 85% capacitance after 1,00,000 cycles at ∼3 A/g.

These results highlight coal-derived graphite foam as an effective precursor for exfoliated coal-derived graphene, which enhances electrode conductivity, capacitance, and power density, making it a promising additive for advanced supercapacitors.
